items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon / CER claim: why do sudden changes in the direction or speed of a roller coaster affect its riders?

body.html: Known: acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity changes when speed changes or when direction changes. Need: a claim, evidence, and reasoning. Use illustrative numbers: a coaster car moving at +20 m/s goes around a hairpin turn and ends up moving at −20 m/s along the same line in 2.5 s.
Acceleration is ¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡. A large velocity change in a short time means a large acceleration, and the riders' bodies must be accelerated along with the car.

This is about 1.6 times 𝑔 (16 / 9.8 ≈1.6). Evidence: (1) acceleration occurs whenever speed changes or direction changes; (2) the track curves, so the direction changes even if the speed does not; (3) a small 𝛥𝑡 makes ¯𝑎 large.

answer.html: Claim: sudden changes in speed or direction are large accelerations (large 𝛥𝑣 in small 𝛥𝑡), and riders feel pushed or pulled during large accelerations. Evidence: ¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡 with both speed changes and direction changes counting; in the example ¯𝑎= −16 m/s<sup>2</sup> ≈1.6𝑔. Reasoning: the shorter the time for a given velocity change, the greater the acceleration. (Exact effects on the body involve forces, covered later.)

check.html: Reversing direction at constant speed still gives 𝛥𝑣≠0, so the acceleration is nonzero.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: "Ask Questions" (add questions to the driving question board)

question.html: Your class is looking at photos of a roller coaster's loop and drop. This is a personal activity with no single answer. Example questions that fit the module: How many times larger than 𝑔 is the acceleration in the tightest turn? Why does the stomach feel different at the top of a hill than at the bottom? How does the time it takes to change direction change what riders feel?

answer.html: Open-ended; sample questions above (no calculation required).

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (after Figure 2): A motion diagram of a skater shows velocity vectors that get longer for three steps, stay the same length for two steps, and then get shorter for three steps. What does each stage indicate?

body.html: On a motion diagram the length of a velocity vector stands for speed.
Longer vectors mean increasing speed; equal-length vectors mean constant speed; shorter vectors mean decreasing speed.

answer.html: The skater speeds up, then glides at constant speed, then slows down.

check.html: The spacing of the dots would also grow, stay equal, then shrink.

items.title: Lesson 1, Analyze (after Figure 3): A lab cart's motion diagram shows two successive velocity vectors with the same length (1.2 m/s) but pointing in opposite directions, 0.50 s apart (the cart bounced off a spring). Can you draw an acceleration vector? What is it?

body.html: Take the first direction as positive: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = + 1.2 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = −1.2 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 0.50 s.
The acceleration vector is 𝛥→𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡 with 𝛥→𝑣= →𝑣<sub>f</sub> −→𝑣<sub>i</sub>. Equal lengths do not make 𝛥→𝑣 zero if the directions differ.
Place −→𝑣<sub>i</sub> tail-to-tip with →𝑣<sub>f</sub>: both point in the negative direction, so they add.

answer.html: Yes. The acceleration vector has magnitude 4.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and points in the negative direction (the direction of →𝑣<sub>f</sub>, opposite the original motion).

check.html: The velocity changed sign, so the change in velocity (−2.4 m/s) is twice the speed, not zero.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 4 discussion): Describe the motion of an object whose velocity is −6.0 m/s while its acceleration is +1.5 m/s

body.html: When 𝑣 and 𝑎 point in opposite directions, 𝑎 reduces the magnitude of 𝑣.
After 2.0 s: 𝑣= −6.0 + (1.5)(2.0) = −3.0 m/s, a smaller speed. The velocity reaches zero at 𝑡= 6.0 / 1.5 = 4.0 s, and after that it becomes positive and grows.

answer.html: The object is slowing down (moving in the negative direction at decreasing speed); if the acceleration continues it stops after 4.0 s and then speeds up in the positive direction.

check.html: Opposite signs of 𝑣 and 𝑎 always mean slowing down.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Velocity-time graphs, Figure 5): The velocity-time graph of a cart is a straight line sloping downward, from 8.0 m/s at 0 s to 2.0 m/s at 3.0 s. What can you conclude about its acceleration?

body.html: Acceleration is the slope of a 𝑣-𝑡 graph; a straight line has the same slope everywhere.

answer.html: The acceleration is constant, at −2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> (the cart is steadily slowing down).

check.html: The negative slope matches the cart losing 2.0 m/s each second.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 6): A velocity-time graph for a toy car crosses the time axis at 3.5 s, going from positive to negative values. What does the crossing mean?

body.html: The vertical axis is velocity, so crossing the time axis means 𝑣= 0 and a change of sign.
Before 3.5 s the velocity is positive, after it is negative. At 3.5 s the car is momentarily at rest and then moves in the opposite direction.

answer.html: At 3.5 s the velocity is zero and changes sign, so the car reverses its direction of motion. Its acceleration need not be zero at that instant.

check.html: A graph that only touches the axis without crossing would mean the car stops but does not reverse.

items.title: Lesson 1, Calculate (Figure 7): A scooter's velocity is recorded in the table below. How large is its average acceleration between 0.00 s and 3.00 s?

body.html: 𝑣= 0.0 m/s at 0.00 s and 𝑣= 5.4 m/s at 3.00 s. Find ¯𝑎.
Average acceleration is the slope between two points on the 𝑣-𝑡 graph.

answer.html: 1.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> (in the positive direction)

check.html: The velocity gains grow each second (0.6, 1.8, 3.0, 4.2), and 1.8 falls between the smallest and the largest gain per second in the first 3 s.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Instantaneous acceleration): For the scooter above, the average acceleration from 0.00 s to 3.00 s is 1.8 m/s

question.html: 2. A tangent line to the 𝑣-𝑡 curve at 𝑡= 3.00 s passes through (2.00 s, 1.8 m/s) and (4.00 s, 9.0 m/s). How is the instantaneous acceleration at 3.00 s different from the average?

body.html: Average acceleration uses the whole interval (slope of a chord); instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent at one instant.

answer.html: The instantaneous acceleration at 3.00 s is 3.6 m/s<sup>2</sup>, twice the average of 1.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, because the acceleration is increasing. The two are equal only when the acceleration is constant.

check.html: The scooter's acceleration is smaller early in the interval, so the average over the interval must be less than the value at the end.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Calculating acceleration): A ball rolls toward a wall at 6.0 m/s and rebounds at 4.5 m/s in 0.30 s. If toward the wall is positive, explain why the final velocity used in the equation is −4.5 m/s, and find the average acceleration.

body.html: Velocity is a vector; the sign shows direction.
After the rebound the ball moves away from the wall, opposite the chosen positive direction, so 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = −4.5 m/s.

answer.html: The final motion is away from the wall (the negative direction), so 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = −4.5 m/s. The average acceleration is −35 m/s<sup>2</sup>, i.e. 35 m/s<sup>2</sup> directed away from the wall.

check.html: 𝛥𝑣= −10.5 m/s is larger than either speed, which is typical when direction reverses.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1 (Figure 8): A cyclist's velocity changes as follows: speeds up uniformly from rest to 5.0 m/s during the first 2.0 s; stays at 5.0 m/s from 2.0 s to 4.0 s; slows uniformly to 1.0 m/s from 4.0 s to 5.0 s; holds 1.0 m/s from 5.0 s to 7.0 s; then slows uniformly to rest from 7.0 s to 8.0 s. Sketch the motion diagram, including velocity vectors, with dots every 1.0 s.

body.html: Velocity at each second: 0, 2.5, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0 m/s for 𝑡= 0 to 8 s. The cyclist always moves in the same direction.
Dot spacing and vector length both represent speed; the time between dots is equal.

Distance between successive dots equals the average speed in that second: 1.25, 3.75, 5.0, 5.0, 3.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.5 m. So the dots start close together and spread out (speeding up), are equal and widest (constant speed), then bunch up and are equal and close (slow constant speed), then bunch up again at the end.

answer.html: Vectors lengthen, then stay long and equal, then shorten, then stay short and equal, then shrink to zero; all point the same way. Dot spacing follows the same pattern (sketch above).

check.html: The total of the spacings is 20.5 m, and the dots are never reversed.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 2 (Figure 9): A toy tram's velocity-time graph is shown (see the figure and the values): 𝑣 rises steadily from 0 to 8.0 m/s in 0-4.0 s; stays at 8.0 m/s from 4.0 to 12.0 s; falls to 2.0 m/s at 16.0 s; then curves gently down to 0 at 30.0 s. (a) When is the tram moving at constant speed? (b) When is its acceleration positive? (c) When is its acceleration most negative?

body.html: Values as stated above (the last stretch is a gentle curve that ends with a shallow slope).
Constant speed means a horizontal line (slope 0). Positive acceleration means the line slopes upward. The most negative acceleration is the steepest downward slope.
14.0 s (average −0.14 m/s<sup>2</sup>), far gentler.
(a) The graph is horizontal between 4.0 s and 12.0 s.
(b) The graph slopes up only from 0 to 4.0 s.
(c) Slope from 12.0 to 16.0 s: (2.0 −8.0) / 4.0 = −1.5 m/s2. The last curve only drops 2.0 m/s in

answer.html: (a) 4.0 s to 12.0 s (speed 8.0 m/s).
(c) 12.0 s to 16.0 s (slope about −1.5 m/s2).

check.html: The steepest downward line on the graph is the 12-16 s segment.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 3 (Figure 9): For the same tram, the velocity is 𝑣(0) = 0, 𝑣(4.0 s) = 8.0 m/s, 𝑣(12.0 s) = 8.0 m/s, 𝑣(16.0 s) = 2.0 m/s, 𝑣(30.0 s) = 0. Find the average acceleration over (a) 0.0-4.0 s, (b) 12.0-16.0 s, and (c) the whole 30.0 s trip.

body.html: The values in the problem; find ¯𝑎 for each interval.
¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡.
(c) The tram starts and ends at rest, so 𝛥𝑣= 0.

answer.html: (c) 0 m/s2 (the average over the whole trip is zero even though the acceleration was not zero during it)

check.html: Signs match the slopes (up, down, net zero).

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 4 (Challenge): A mine cage descends from rest. Taking up as positive, it first has acceleration −0.60 m/s

question.html: 2 for 2.5 s, then moves at constant velocity for 10.0 s, then has acceleration +0.30 m/s2 for 5.0 s and stops. Plot its velocity-time graph.

body.html: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = 0. Phase 1: 𝑎= −0.60 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 2.5 s. Phase 2: constant velocity, 10.0 s. Phase 3: 𝑎= + 0.30 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 5.0 s.
𝑣<sub>f</sub> = 𝑣<sub>i</sub> + 𝑎𝛥𝑡 gives the corner points of the graph.
Constant until 𝑡= 2.5 + 10.0 = 12.5 s. Then

answer.html: Straight segments joining (0, 0), (2.5 s, −1.5 m/s), (12.5 s, −1.5 m/s), (17.5 s, 0) .

check.html: The cage ends at rest, and the velocity is negative the whole time because it moves down.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 5: A sports car speeds up from 5.0 m/s to 29 m/s in 4.5 s. What is its average acceleration?

body.html: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = 5.0 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = 29 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 4.5 s. Find ¯𝑎.
Definition of average acceleration.

answer.html: 5.3 m/s<sup>2</sup> forward

check.html: Positive, since the car speeds up in the positive direction.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 6: A speedboat slows from 27 m/s to 9.0 m/s in 5.0 s. What is its average acceleration?

body.html: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = 27 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = 9.0 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 5.0 s.

answer.html: −3.6 m/s<sup>2</sup> (that is, 3.6 m/s<sup>2</sup> opposite the direction of motion)

check.html: Negative while moving forward means slowing down.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 7: A tram traveling north at 18 m/s brakes to a stop in 4.5 s. (a) What is its average acceleration? (b) If a gentler stop took 7.5 s, what would the average acceleration be?

body.html: Choose north as positive: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = + 18 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = 0.
¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡.

answer.html: (a) −4.0 m/s2, i.e. 4.0 m/s2 directed south (opposite the tram's motion)
(b) −2.4 m/s2 (2.4 m/s2 south), smaller in magnitude than in part (a)

check.html: For the same 𝛥𝑣, a longer time gives a smaller acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 8: A cart rolling on a ramp moves down the ramp at 1.9 m/s. After 1.8 s it is moving up the ramp at 2.6 m/s. Find its average acceleration.

body.html: Up the ramp positive: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = −1.9 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = + 2.6 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 1.8 s.

answer.html: +2.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> (up the ramp)

check.html: The cart first slows (moving down) then speeds up moving up, both consistent with an up- ramp acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 9: A hiker walking west slows from 2.40 m/s to 0.65 m/s in 8.0 s. Find the average acceleration.

body.html: West positive: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = + 2.40 m/s, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = + 0.65 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 8.0 s.

answer.html: −0.22 m/s<sup>2</sup> (i.e. 0.22 m/s<sup>2</sup> east)

check.html: Slowing while moving west requires an eastward (negative) acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 10 (Challenge): A glacier's flow speed slows from 75 m/y to 45 m/y over 2.0 y. Find the average acceleration in m/y

body.html: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = 75 m/y, 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = 45 m/y, 𝛥𝑡= 2.0 y.
Convert: 1 y = 3.156 × 10<sup>7</sup> s, so 1 y<sup>2</sup> = 9.96 × 10<sup>14</sup> s<sup>2</sup>:

answer.html: −15 m/y<sup>2</sup>, which is about −1.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>14</sup> m/s<sup>2</sup>

check.html: The glacier moves so slowly that its acceleration in m/s<sup>2</sup> is astronomically small.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Acceleration with constant speed): A car drives around a circular track at a constant 20 m/s. Describe the evidence that the car is accelerating even though its speed is constant, and find the magnitude of its average acceleration if its velocity turns from east to north in 5.0 s.

body.html: Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction.

The car's direction keeps changing, so its velocity vector changes even though its length (speed) does not. From east at 20 m/s to north at 20 m/s, the change in velocity is the diagonal of a right triangle with legs 20 m/s: 𝛥𝑣= √(20 m/s)<sup>2</sup> + (20 m/s)<sup>2</sup> = 28 m/s,

answer.html: The car's direction changes, so its velocity changes and it is accelerating at constant speed. The average acceleration over this quarter-turn is 5.7 m/s<sup>2</sup>, pointing toward the inside of the curve (northwest).

check.html: A change in direction of 90° at 20 m/s is a larger velocity change than either vector alone.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 11: A cyclist's velocity can change in three different ways. Name them and give a numeric example of each.

body.html: Acceleration is any change in velocity (a vector).

Velocity changes if its magnitude increases, its magnitude decreases, or its direction changes. Examples: speeding up from 4 m/s to 8 m/s; slowing from 8 m/s to 4 m/s; riding around a corner at a constant 6 m/s.

answer.html: (1) Speeding up, (2) slowing down, (3) changing direction (even at constant speed).

check.html: These cover every way 𝛥→𝑣 can be nonzero.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 12 (Figure 10): Two cyclists both ride east at a constant 5.0 m/s. At 𝑡= 0 cyclist 1 is 20 m west of a tree (𝑥= −20 m) and cyclist 2 is 10 m east of it (𝑥= + 10 m). (a) Describe their position-time graphs and give each position at 𝑡= 4.0 s. (b) Describe their velocity-time graphs.

body.html: East positive, 𝑣= + 5.0 m/s for both, 𝑥<sub>i,1</sub> = −20 m, 𝑥<sub>i,2</sub> = + 10 m.
Position: 𝑥= 𝑥<sub>i</sub> + 𝑣𝑡. At 4.0 s: 𝑥<sub>1</sub> = −20 + (5.0)(4.0) = 0 m and 𝑥<sub>2</sub> = 10 + (5.0)(4.0) = 30 m.

answer.html: The position-time graphs are parallel straight lines with the same slope (5.0 m/s), differing only in their 𝑥-intercepts (−20 m and +10 m, a 30 m offset). At 4.0 s they are at 0 m and 30 m.
The velocity-time graphs are identical: the same horizontal line at +5.0 m/s (they lie on top of one another).

check.html: A 𝑣-𝑡 graph holds no information about starting position.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 13: Sketch the velocity-time graph for a truck that travels north at 18 m/s for 60 s, then south at 12 m/s for 90 s.

body.html: North positive: 𝑣= + 18 m/s for 0-60 s, then 𝑣= −12 m/s for 60-150 s. Both are horizontal lines (zero acceleration within each part).

answer.html: A horizontal line at +18 m/s from 0 to 60 s, then a horizontal line at −12 m/s from 60 to 150 s (a sudden jump across the axis at 60 s).

check.html: The speed changes and the velocity changes sign at 60 s.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 14: A kayaker paddles upstream at 1.8 m/s for 5.0 s, then drifts downstream at 3.2 m/s for 7.0 s. (a) Find the average velocity over the whole 12.0 s. (b) Find the average acceleration over the whole 12.0 s.

body.html: Downstream positive: 𝑣<sub>1</sub> = −1.8 m/s for 5.0 s, 𝑣<sub>2</sub> = + 3.2 m/s for 7.0 s.
¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡; ¯𝑎= (𝑣<sub>f</sub> −𝑣<sub>i</sub>) / 𝛥𝑡 using the initial and final velocities.
(b) Taking the velocity at the start (−1.8) and at the end (+3.2 m/s):

answer.html: (a) 1.1 m/s downstream
(b) 0.42 m/s2 downstream (this is an average; the velocity change really happens in a short time at the 5.0 s mark).

check.html: Average velocity is not the average of the speeds; direction matters.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (Critical Thinking): A jogger and a cyclist travel along the same path. At 𝑡= 3 s they are side by side, and the jogger says, "We are next to each other, so we must have the same velocity." Positions (m) at each second are: jogger 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 and cyclist 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 for 𝑡= 0 to 6 s. Is the jogger correct?

body.html: Being next to each other means equal position at one instant. It says nothing about velocity, which is how position changes.
Jogger: each second the position changes by 2 m, so 𝑣= 2.0 m/s. Cyclist: changes by 4 m each second, so 𝑣= 4.0 m/s. Both are at 12 m at 𝑡= 3 s. Before that the cyclist was behind; after, ahead.

answer.html: The jogger is not correct. Equal position at one instant does not mean equal velocity. The cyclist's dots are twice as far apart (4.0 m/s versus 2.0 m/s), so the cyclist passes the jogger at 3 s.

check.html: If their velocities were equal, they would stay side by side; they do not.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon / CER claim: why do sudden changes in the direction or speed of jet planes affect pilots?

body.html: Known: the module defines acceleration as a change in velocity, and velocity changes when speed changes or when direction changes. Need: a claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Acceleration is ¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡. A large velocity change in a short time means a large acceleration, and the pilot's body must be accelerated along with the plane.
Illustrative numbers (made up for this explanation, not from the book): a jet moving at +250 m/s reverses to −250 m/s in 10 s.

This is about 5 times 𝑔 (50 / 9.8 ≈5.1). Evidence from the module: (1) acceleration occurs whenever speed changes or direction changes; (2) the planes in the photo leave curved trails, so their directions change even if their speeds do not; (3) a small 𝛥𝑡 makes ¯𝑎 large.

answer.html: Claim: sudden changes in speed or direction are large accelerations (large 𝛥𝑣 in small 𝛥𝑡), and a pilot's body feels pushed or pulled during large accelerations. Evidence: ¯𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡, with speed changes and direction changes both counting. Reasoning: the shorter the time for a given velocity change, the greater the acceleration. (Exact effects on the body come from forces, which later modules treat.)

check.html: A change of direction at constant speed still gives 𝛥𝑣≠0, so acceleration is nonzero, consistent with the module's wind-sprint example.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: "Ask Questions" (add questions to the driving question board)

question.html: This is a personal class activity with no single answer. Example questions that fit the module: How large is the acceleration of a jet in a tight turn compared with 𝑔? How long can a person tolerate a given acceleration? Does speeding up feel different from turning?

answer.html: Open-ended; sample questions above (no calculation required).

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (after Figure 2): What do increasing and decreasing lengths of velocity vectors indicate?

body.html: On a motion diagram the velocity vector's length stands for speed.
If each successive vector is longer, speed is increasing; if each is shorter, speed is decreasing.

answer.html: Increasing vector lengths mean the object is speeding up; decreasing lengths mean it is slowing down.

check.html: Matches Figure 2, where the dot spacing also grows or shrinks.

items.title: Lesson 1, Analyze (after Figure 3): Can you draw an acceleration vector for two successive velocity vectors that are the same length and direction?

body.html: The acceleration vector is 𝛥→𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡 with 𝛥→𝑣= →𝑣<sub>f</sub> −→𝑣<sub>i</sub>.
If →𝑣<sub>f</sub> = →𝑣<sub>i</sub>, then 𝛥→𝑣= →𝑣<sub>f</sub> + ( −→𝑣<sub>i</sub>) = 0. Placing −→𝑣<sub>i</sub> tail-to-tip with →𝑣<sub>f</sub> closes back on itself, so the vector has zero length.

answer.html: No. The change in velocity is zero, so the acceleration is zero and there is no vector to draw (uniform motion).

check.html: Uniform motion means constant velocity, which means zero acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 4 discussion): Describe the motion of an object if its velocity and acceleration vectors have opposite signs.

body.html: When 𝑣 and 𝑎 point in opposite directions, 𝑎 reduces the magnitude of 𝑣.
Example: 𝑣= + 10 m/s, 𝑎= −2 m/s<sup>2</sup>. After 1 s, 𝑣= + 8 m/s: smaller speed. If the acceleration continues, the object stops momentarily and then speeds up in the opposite direction.

answer.html: The object is slowing down (and, if the acceleration continues, will stop and then reverse direction).

check.html: Same as the ball rolling up the driveway in Example Problem 2.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Velocity-time graphs, Figure 5): What can you conclude about the acceleration if the graph is a straight line on a velocity-time graph?

body.html: Acceleration is the slope of a 𝑣-𝑡 graph.
A straight line has the same slope everywhere.

answer.html: The acceleration is constant (uniform acceleration).

check.html: Figure 5 has a constant slope of 5.00 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 6): Describe the meaning of a line crossing the x-axis in a velocity-time graph.

body.html: The vertical axis is velocity, so crossing the time axis means 𝑣= 0 and a sign change.
Above the axis the velocity is positive; below it is negative. At the crossing point the object is momentarily at rest and then moves in the opposite direction (like Graph D).

answer.html: The velocity is zero at that instant and changes sign, so the object reverses its direction of motion.

check.html: The object is momentarily at rest, but its acceleration need not be zero.

items.title: Lesson 1, Calculate (Figure 7): How large is the average acceleration between 0.00 s and 2.00 s?

body.html: From Figure 7: 𝑣= 0 at 𝑡= 0.00 s and 𝑣= 4.0 m/s at 𝑡= 2.00 s. Find ¯𝑎.
Average acceleration is the slope of the 𝑣-𝑡 graph between two points.

answer.html: 2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> (in the positive direction)

check.html: The slope is gentle near 𝑡= 0 and steeper later, so a modest average of 2.0 over this early interval fits.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Instantaneous acceleration): How is instantaneous acceleration different from average acceleration?

body.html: Average acceleration uses the whole interval; instantaneous acceleration uses a single instant.
Average: 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡 over a chosen interval (the slope of a chord). Instantaneous: the slope of the tangent line at one time.

answer.html: Average acceleration is the total velocity change divided by the time interval. Instantaneous acceleration is the acceleration at one instant, found from the slope of the tangent to the 𝑣-𝑡 curve. They are equal only when acceleration is constant.

check.html: In Example Problem 1 the instantaneous values (2.9 and 0.030 m/s<sup>2</sup>) differ widely.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Calculating acceleration): Explain why the final velocity used in the equation is −4.0 m/s.

body.html: Velocity is a vector; sign shows direction.
Positive was chosen toward the wall. At the end you run away from the wall, which is the negative direction, with speed 4.0 m/s, so 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = −4.0 m/s.

answer.html: Because the final motion is away from the wall, opposite the chosen positive direction (toward the wall), the velocity is negative: 𝑣<sub>f</sub> = −4.0 m/s.

check.html: This gives 𝛥𝑣= −8.0 m/s, matching the book's −0.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1 (Figure 8): Sketch the motion diagram for Steven's v-t graph, including velocity vectors.

body.html: Figure 8 (no numbers on the velocity axis): constant positive velocity from 0 to 2 s; decreasing to a smaller positive constant 3-5 s; decreasing to zero 5-6 s; zero from 6 to 7 s; sharp rise 7-8 s to a velocity larger than the start; constant 8-10 s. All velocities are ≥0, so he always moves in one direction.
Dot spacing and vector length both represent speed; equal time between dots.

I chose representative speeds (not read from the graph, which has no scale): 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 4, 4 units. Dots are one second apart. Spacing: equal (0-2 s), shrinking (2-3 s), equal and smaller (3-5 s), shrinking to zero (5-6 s), dots on top of each other (6-7 s), spreading quickly (7-8 s), equal and largest (8-10 s).

answer.html: Equal-length vectors, then shorter vectors, then equal shorter vectors, then vectors shrinking to zero, then no spacing (at rest), then a long vector jump, then equal long vectors; all point the same way. (Sketch above; lengths are qualitative.)

check.html: The final speed is greater than the starting speed, as on the graph.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Acceleration with constant speed): Describe the evidence that the planes at the start of the module are accelerating even at constant speed.

body.html: Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction.
The planes' skywriting trails are curved, so the planes' directions change, so the velocity vector changes even if speed is constant.

answer.html: The curved trails show the planes' direction of motion is changing, so their velocity changes and they are accelerating even at constant speed.

check.html: Same idea as running back and forth across the gym at 4.0 m/s.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 11: What are three ways an object can accelerate?

body.html: Acceleration is any change in velocity (a vector).
Velocity changes if its magnitude increases, its magnitude decreases, or its direction changes.

answer.html: (1) Speeding up, (2) slowing down, (3) changing direction (even at constant speed).

check.html: These cover every way 𝛥→𝑣 can be nonzero.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 12 (Figure 10): two joggers at 7.5 m/s east

body.html: Both have 𝑣= + 7.5 m/s (east positive). Figure 10: jogger 1 starts at 15 m west (𝑥= −15 m), jogger 2 at 15 m east (𝑥= + 15 m) at 𝑡= 0.
Position: 𝑥= 𝑥<sub>i</sub> + 𝑣𝑡. Same slope (7.5 m/s), different intercepts. Velocity: both are constant at 7.5 m/s.

answer.html: The two position-time graphs are parallel straight lines with the same slope (7.5 m/s); they differ only in their 𝑥-intercepts: one starts at −15 m, the other at +15 m (a 30 m offset).
The velocity-time graphs are identical: the same horizontal line at +7.5 m/s (they lie on top of one another).

check.html: A 𝑣-𝑡 graph holds no information about starting position.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (Critical Thinking): the speeding driver and the slower car

body.html: Being next to each other means equal position at one instant. It says nothing about velocity, which is how position changes.

Sketch two cars side by side at 𝑡= 2 in the diagram: the speeding car's dots are spaced farther apart (longer vectors) than the slower car's, yet at 𝑡= 2 both dots sit at the same position. A moment before, the speeding car was behind; a moment later, it is ahead.

answer.html: The driver is not correct. Cars observed next to each other have the same position at that instant, but their speeds can differ. The motion diagram shows the speeder's dots farther apart (greater speed) even though both cars occupy the same spot at one time, so the other driver was slower and was passed.

check.html: If speeds were equal, the cars would stay side by side; they do not.
